source_text: Quid ergo? Acquiescam prorsus tibi, faciamque in hoc loco iacturam omnium, quorum adminiculo uti possem, contentusque ero definitione, quae ad indicium bonae naturae post Manichaeorum secretum de ore tuae honestatis effugit. In eo igitur libro cui titulus est, vel De duabus animabus, vel Contra duas animas, ita loqueris: Exspecta, sine prius peccatum definiamus. Peccatum est voluntas admittendi vel retinendi quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere. Quamquam si liberum non est, nec voluntas dici potest; sed malui grossius, quam scrupulosius definire [n40] .
pass_a_gloss: What then? I will acquiesce to you outright, and in this place I will make a loss of all whose support I could use, and I will be content with a definition which, as an indication of a good nature, fled from the mouth of your honesty after the secret of the Manichaeans. In that book therefore whose title is either On the two souls or Against the two souls, you speak thus: Wait, allow first that we define sin. Sin is a will of admitting or retaining what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. Although if it is not free, it cannot even be called will; but I preferred to define more roughly than more scrupulously.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil

pass_b_english: What then? I will indeed yield to you. At this point I will give up everyone whose support I could use and be content with a definition which, as evidence of a good nature, escaped from your honorable mouth after you left the secret company of the Manichaeans. In the book entitled either On Two Souls or Against Two Souls, you say: “Wait; let us first define sin. Sin is the will to commit or retain something justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain. In fact, if one is not free, it cannot even be called will; but I preferred a rougher definition to a more exacting one” (Augustine, On Two Souls 15).

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
